Drums are precisely tuned and played melodically; caption documents wooden-stick playing and a set of four differently sized skin-covered drums in the pictured subset. Four skin-drum musicians does not mean only four total drums. All five players and both sound families are retained. This is the whole separately documented original6(a) performance, not the adjacent6(b) national celebration or the entire multi-ethnic album. Digital track206 combines both sub-selections; no unverified digital edit timestamp is supplied. A single whole skin-drum-ensemble card retains all four players and their multiple tuned drums; exact individual drum counts, dimensions, tuning frequencies and shell material remain unspecified. It is not replaced with the existing conical hand-played igba. The hollow-log role uses existing Igbo ekwe with authored medium two-tone size and interlocking dance support; size, pitch count and exact timeline are editorial choices, not measured original parameters. The documented instrumental orchestra has zero separately credited singers; incidental crowd sounds are not claimed absent. record.description: Ladislav Bihari — Spievanky, spievanky, complete one-page heligónka arrangement issued by Miroslav Jurči / Pesničky pre všetkých. The specific score is for a two-row C/F instrument and retains the entire right-hand melody and harmonization, left-hand bass/chords, button choices and push/pull bellows directions. It is an authored instrumental realization of this complete instrumental arrangement, not a reconstruction of an unspecified vocal recording. Printed song lyrics and six verses remain source underlay/context; the publisher identifies the arrangement for heligónka, not a separate scored singer. No additional vocalist is inferred from printed words. The institutionally documented one-player heligónka practice supports this single-player realization; no claim all heligónka music is instrumental. Broad functionalSong represents the selected strophic folk-song melody and explicitly notated functional C/D-minor/F/G7 chord cycle, realized instrumentally across its verses. This does not imply Anglosphere pop/rock or through-composed concert art solely because a score exists. The isolated free-reed owner preserves four documented physical/playing dimensions: two C/F rows with eleven and ten right-hand buttons; a sixth-button F-row stoják retaining one pitch in both bellows directions; left-hand bass-plus-chord support; and explicitly scored push/pull melody phrasing. No manufacturer, reed metal, reed rank count, shell material or measured original tuning frequency is invented. Stoják-present option is selected from the score’s documented alternatives. Authored controlled live-room realization and equal-tempered baseline are editorial recording choices, not a source-session claim.

existing_record.name: Musique traditionnelle québécoise
existing_record.lineage: Québec's French-Canadian dance and song tradition of the Saint Lawrence valley, documented from the nineteenth century, professionalized by La Bolduc and fiddler Jean Carignan and revived from the 1970s by La Bottine Souriante and Le Vent du Nord — crooked reels and gigues at 110-130 BPM driven by seated podorythmie foot percussion, diatonic accordion and fiddle in unison, ragtime-inflected piano backing, and chansons à répondre with turlutte mouth-music refrains.

existing_extras.description: Traditional Québécois music is the kitchen-party and veillée repertoire of French Canada, built on fiddle-and-accordion dance tunes and responsorial song, and continuously performed rather than reconstructed. Its unmistakable features are podorythmie — the fiddler's own seated foot-tapping as the rhythm section — irregular 'crooked' tune structures with added or dropped beats, a piano accompaniment style borrowed from ragtime and vaudeville, and turlutte vocal mouth-music standing in for instruments. It shares Celtic modal tune shapes with Irish and Cape Breton traditions but is distinguished by the foot-percussion drive, the French song layer, and the tolerance for asymmetrical bar counts that Scottish and Irish repertoires largely regularized away.
